687.dq: Lealao phonological words consist minimally of a single stressed syllable and may have up to five unstressed syllables preceding the stressed syllable and one unstressed syllable following. (Rupp 1989:1)
687.dloc: Rupp 1989 ch.1 pp.1 and 3 (sections 1, 1.4) [pp.15,17]; Rupp ms p.1 [p.2]
687.heavy: none; no weight criterion for stress placement is stated (vowel length and checked/unchecked syllables are discussed only as phonetic correlates of the ballistic/controlled stress-type contrast)
687.prule: One stressed syllable per phonological word; it is the root syllable. Prefixes (up to five syllables, on verbs) are unstressed; at most one unstressed syllable (a person-marker) may follow the stressed root. Stress TYPE on that syllable is lexically ballistic vs controlled (minimal pairs).
687.srule: None: one stress per phonological word - 'a unit constituted of syllables of which only one is stressed' (Rupp 1990:63 = ms p.1); pretonic prefix syllables and the one possible posttonic person-marker syllable are unstressed (Rupp 1989:1); a posttonic person marker may be lexically marked ballistic for tone sandhi but is 'pronounced without stress' (Rupp 1990:72).

687.idn: Lealao Chinantec, the Chinantec language of San Juan Lealao, ex-District of Choapan, northeast Oaxaca, Mexico (also a few speakers in Santa María Yahuivé and Latani); data: 'Data for this paper were collected between 1968 and 1981, during which time I resided in Lealao, with my wife and two daughters, for a total…
687.exq_: Most Chinantec words have simple roots or stems. Thus, though they may occur with several prefixes (as with verbs) the root of the word is readily identified as the syllable that receives stress—whether controlled or ballistic.
687.tone: yes: four level tones (low, mid, high, very high) and two upglides (low-mid, low-high); only the level tones occur with ballistic stress; anticipatory/perseverative tone raising (Rupp 1989:3-4, 1.5)

dfl.q: The phonological word is typically just one stressed syllable, although a verb may be realized phonologically as a string of as many as six syllables. The stressed syllable is the last syllable of the word unless the word ends with one of five unstressed person markers.

tn.quote: 1.5. Tone. Lealao Chinantec has four level tones (low, mid, high, very high) and two upglides (low-mid and low-high). Only the level tones may occur with ballistic stress. Examples are: me:ⱽᴴ 'Demetrius', mé:ⱽᴴ 'leaf cutter ants', me:ᴴ 'flea', mé:ᴴ 'liquor', me:ᴹ 'leaf', ŋiú:ᴹ 'many', me:ᴸ 'egg', mé:ᴸ 'sharp', me:ᴸᴹ 'he rubs it', me:ᴸᴴ 'rub it!'. ... [fn.1, p.1] Tone is indicated in this study by /L/ (low), /M/ (mid), /H/ (high), /VH/ (very high), and by combinations of the first three of these, as in /LH/ (low-high).

688.heavy: long vowels only ([+long] vowel syllables = heavy); closed syllables (coda consonants, including geminates) are explicitly NOT heavy ('coda consonants are stress-insensitive', 'consonants in Leti are non-moraic').
688.dflt: penultimate (the rule is penultimate regardless of weight)
688.prule: Word stress falls on the (fixed) penultimate syllable of the lexeme (Hume: 'word stress falls on the penultimate syllable'; van Engelenhoven: foot = '(fixed) stress-bearing vowel in the penultimate syllable of the lexeme'). In connected speech the last foot of the phonological phrase ('section') carries main stress.
688.srule: In concatenations of roots and words within the phonological phrase ('section'), the penultimate stresses of the non-final lexical roots surface as secondary stresses before the main stress on the rightmost root: a light-syllable stress directly preceding the main-stress foot is lost (matrúma *màtrúma, kudmáta), it is retained when at least one unstressed buffer syllable intervenes (pòtaltáni, rùmlaápna, kaBàlkiBnútna), and long-vowel (heavy) syllables are always stressed even in clash (rò:nénu, mà:nwá:na); closed syllables and geminates count as light. Hume: 'secondary stress generally occurring on alternating syllables preceding the main stress... long vowels are always stressed'. A monomorphemic root (at most three syllables, antepenult extrapedal) carries one stress.

689.dq: Otherwise, stress the ultima of a two syllable word beginning a light syllable ... In sum, word stress patterns of Arabic dialects differ along a number of dimensions
689.dloc: Kager 2009 author-MS p. 12, ex. (25b) header and p. 13, 'In sum' paragraph; cf. also p. 2 'All modern Arabic dialects have word stress: one syllable in a word is prominent as compared to other syllables'
689.heavy: Kager (general definition used throughout the article): 'A light syllable is an open syllable that contains a short vowel (CV). A heavy syllable is one that contains a long vowel (CVV) or a short vowel and a consonant (CVC).' Superheavy = CVVC or CVCC; only a SUPERHEAVY ultima attracts stress (final CVC in LLH ka.tá.bat, HLLH in.ga.tá.lat is not stressed), except that an LH disyllable is stressed finally (ka.táb/kitáb). StressTyp2 entry note: 'long vowels; closed syllables'.
689.dflt: by L->R iambic parity over the light string: penult when the penult is an odd number of syllables from the closest preceding heavy syllable or the left word edge (LLL, LLH ka.tá.bat, HLLH in.ga.tá.lat), otherwise antepenult (even-length light strings, e.g. LLLL/LLLH, per Van de Vijver 1996:179 / StressTyp2 entry 'even numbered syllables, counting from the left edge'; Kager's ex. 25e shows only penult cases); a disyllable with a light first syllable is stressed finally (rule b); light monosyllables do not occur (StressTyp2 phonotactic note)
689.prule: (a) stress a superheavy (CVVC/CVCC) ultima; (b) otherwise stress the ultima of a two-syllable word beginning with a light syllable (LH ka.táb -> kitáb; disyllables otherwise initial, HH mák.tab); (c) otherwise stress a heavy penult; (d) otherwise stress a heavy antepenult; (e) otherwise -- Kager's abbreviated wording -- stress the penult (LLH ka.tá.bat -> iktíbat, HLLH in.ga.tá.lat -> inigtílat); the fuller statement carried in StressTyp2 from Van de Vijver 1996:179 after Hayes 1995:228-239 is 'stress the penult or the antepenult, whichever is separated from the closest preceding heavy syllable or the left word edge by an odd number of syllables', i.e. light strings are; Watson 2011 Table 135.1 'Iambs, L > R, <Foot>: Yes', so an even-length light string (LLLL, LLLH) would take antepenult stress. Syncope of a stressed foot-head retracts stress onto the foot's weak syllable (ki.tí.bih -> kít.bih).
689.srule: None on the surface: the left-to-right iambic layer of the Hayes 1995 analysis 'is used only for the sake of defining main stress. Secondary stress is absent on the surface' (StressTyp2 entry). Not mentioned in Kager 2009 (Cyrenaican Jebel section, MS pp. 11-12); Watson 2011:25 leaves secondary stress unexamined; Bobaker 2018:173 reports 'only one stress... no secondary stress at all' for neighbouring Tobruq.

tn.quote: Afroasiatic languages have phonologized pitch into different prosodic systems that vary from a demarcative accent system, e.g. Berber; to a lexical stress system, e.g. Tripoli Arabic; a pitch accent system, e.g. Juba Arabic; and a tone system, e.g. Hausa and Zaar … 5.1 TRIPOLI ARABIC PROSODIC SYSTEM Tripoli Arabic has a lexical stress system, i.e. every content word is stressed on one of its syllables. The place of the stress is not fixed but it is predictable (Pereira 2010: 88-89). The prosodic structure of Tripoli Arabic also involves sentence-level prominence stress

morph.rootq: General statement is a free-accent one: Senn 1966 §52 'Der Wortakzent ist im Litauischen nicht an eine bestimmte Silbe gebunden.' (Dambriūnas et al.: 'The stress can fall on almost any syllable of a word and sometimes one form of a word may carry the stress on a certain syllable whereas another form of the same word will carry the stress on another syllable.') But the detailed rules are stated in terms of stem vs ending and root weight vs prefix: §99 'Bei den zu den drei anderen Klassen gehörigen Hauptwörtern vollzieht sich ein Akzentwechsel zwischen der Endsilbe und einer bestimmten vorhergehenden Silbe ... Klasse 1: fester Akzent; ursprünglich stammbetont ... Klasse 3: ursprünglich…
morph.elicq: Senn's account is normative for the written standard with accent marks and defers to dictionaries for word-level facts: §99 'Unsere hier gegebene Darstellung bezieht sich zunächst nur auf die heutige hl. Schriftsprache'; §395b 'Für den Einzelfall ist jeweils das Wörterbuch nachzuschlagen'; §52 'In der gewöhnlichen Rechtschreibung werden diese Akzentzeichen nicht gesetzt. Zum Lernen der richtigen Betonung sind sie für uns aber unentbehrlich.' For the phonetics of the accents he cites instrumental work: §52 'Eine eingehende Beschreibung der drei primären Haupttöne ... ist zu finden bei Georg Gerullis, Litauische Dialektstudien (Leipzig 1930) S. XXI-LV…

evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: A theoretical (Optimality Theory with Turbidity) account of where the single main accent falls in Standard Lithuanian nouns and adjectives: accent is lexical and mobile, placed by the Basic Accentuation Principle (leftmost underlyingly accented vowel, else leftmost vowel) except that monomoraic 'Saussurean' suffixes carrying an underlying accent pull it from the penult to the final syllable, which the author derives from a right-edge clash of two underlying accents of variable strength (strong H vs weak Hl); data are dictionary accent specifications checked with untrained L1 consultants from V
evidence_works.venue: Glossa: a journal of general linguistics

evidence_works.work: Bakšienė & Jolita Urbanavičienė 2023, Standard Lithuanian (Illustrations of the IPA) (Journal of the International Phonetic Association 54(1): 414-444. doi:10.1017/S0025100323000105)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: Word stress is free and distinctive (minimal pairs by stress place), with optional secondary stresses in words of three or more syllables, and its most stable phonetic cue is longer syllable-centre duration, with f0 and intensity varying by phrase intonation (own data: stressed short vowels about twice as long as unstressed in kìtas/kitàs, pitch and intensity differences small). Two pitch accents, acute and circumflex, contrast only in stressed long syllables; the authors class Lithuanian as a pitch-accent language rather than tonal, note the contrast is systematic today only in diphthong or s
evidence_works.loc: pp. 431-439 (section 'Prosodic system': 'Stress' pp. 431-434, 'Pitch accent (toneme)' pp. 434-439; Tables 6-7, Figures 8-15)
evidence_works.venue: Journal of the International Phonetic Association

evidence_works.work: Gleim & Sören E. Tebay 2022, Reflexes of exponent movement in inflectional morphology: A study in Harmonic Serialism (Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 41: 103-158. doi:10.1007/s11049-022-09543-4)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article restates, from Kushnir 2018, that Lithuanian has one main lexical pitch accent per word placed on any mora, with falling vs rising accents, leftmost accent winning except under Saussure's Law, which moves the accent to a word-final accented ending; it adds that in verbs the Saussurean shift onto 1SG -u and 2SG -i applies across an intervening theme vowel (kasjaú, žinaú). It is a theoretical Harmonic Serialism analysis of that fact with no acoustic or articulatory data, so it confirms the entry's lexical / pitch-accent classification and adds the Saussure's Law detail.

tn.translation: §21.2: For long vowels and diphthongs standard Lithuanian has two intonation types, namely Schleifton (marked with the circumflex) and Stoßton (marked with the acute). ... §52: In Lithuanian the word accent is not bound to a particular syllable. ... But if the main stress falls on a long vowel, two different accent signs are used according to the intonation (priegaidė): 1. the acute (dešininis kirtis) for the falling intonation (Stoßton, Lith. tvirtapradė priegaidė), 2. the circumflex (riestinis kirtis) for the rising intonation (Schleifton or Dehnton, Lith. tvirtagalė priegaidė).
tn.cite: Senn, Alfred. 1966. Handbuch der litauischen Sprache. Band I: Grammatik. Heidelberg: Carl Winter Universitätsverlag.
tn.note: Free lexical word accent; stressed long vowels/diphthongs contrast two intonations, acute (falling) vs circumflex (rising); stressed short syllables take grave. Phonetics after Gerullis 1930.

691.dq: Davis 1973 (opened), transcription note: 'An acute accent over a vowel is used to indicate the syllable bearing primary stress in a word.' (Davis separately describes declarative intonation: 'the pitch remains more or less level at mid and falls on the last strongly stressed syllable in the sen­tence to low', i.e. word stress is distinguished from sentence pitch.)
691.dloc: Hill 2005:24 (sec. 2.2.1) carrying Munro 1990:225; StressTyp2 entry = Munro 1990:224; StressTyp2 entry = Hyman 1977:70; SPA Handbook 1979 p. 442, entry 845 'STRESS' = summary of Bright 1965:345 + Kroeber & Grace 1960:8; Davis 1973 sec. 2 'Notation' p. 3 (transcription note) and p. 88 (intonation passage)
691.heavy: Munro 1990 (carried by Hill 2005:24 and StressTyp2 1308): a long vowel in the first or second syllable attracts stress. Bright 1965:345 (as summarized in SPA 1979:442): (1) a long V in the initial syllable is always stressed; (2) a short V in a CLOSED initial syllable is always stressed if the following syllable has a short V and is open — so an initial closed syllable also attracts stress, under a positional condition (before a light open second syllable). ST1 note ': long vowels' records only the vowel-length criterion.
691.dflt: second syllable in nouns, first in verbs (Munro 1990:224); s2 'usually' when s1 and s2 are both open-short (Bright 1965:345 apud SPA 1979); 'usually initial' with rightward shift under suffixation (Hyman 1977:70); Pre-Cupeño reconstruction: first syllable (Munro 1990:225 apud Hill 2005:24)
691.prule: Stress falls within the first two syllables of the word. Munro 1990:224 (carried): stress a long vowel in syllable 1 or 2; if neither is long, stress the second syllable in nouns and the first in verbs (Pre-Cupeño reconstruction: else first syllable, Munro 1990:225 apud Hill 2005:24). Bright 1965:345 (summarized by SPA 1979:442): a long V in s1 is always stressed; a short V in a closed s1 is always stressed when s2 is short and open; if s1 and s2 are both open with short V, s2 is 'usually' stressed; otherwise stress 'may be on either the first or second syllable', the residue being 'morphologically conditioned' (KCG 1960:8: in verbs certain suffixes retract stress to s2; reduplication may also affect stress; Hyman 1977:70: stress 'usually initial', jumping one syllable right to the stem boundary when a bisyllabic stem is suffixed).
691.srule: Not mentioned in the record's carriers (SPA Handbook 1979:442 entry 845; Hill 2005:24; StressTyp2 'No information'). Hill & Hill 2019 (sec. 4.4.3): the stress rule applies to the pronominal prefix as well as to the stem (and to each copy of a doubled root, e.g. nèchinéchax); Rule 12 makes all but the rightmost stress secondary, so prefixes carry a secondary stress that 'usually goes unnoted' in transcription. No rhythmic secondary stress is described ('Little is known about secondary stress', sec. 3.4).
691.quote: Hill 2005:24 [opened]: 'Munro (1990) argues that Proto-Cupan— the Takic community ancestral to Cupeño, Cahuilla, and Luiseño—exhibited a quantity-sensitive stress rule, which is still observed in Luiseño. If not, stress the second syllable in nouns, or stress the first in verbs.' ... SPA 1…

If not, stress the first syllable' is Hill's statement of Munro's 'Pre-Cupeño' reconstruction, not the Luiseño default…

tn.quote: Luiseño is relatively simple as American languages go. It has no tone/pitch, no ergativity and no incorporation, and is vaguely reminiscent of Latin, to which it is certainly more similar structurally than to Navaho, for example.

tn.note: No tone or pitch distinctions; stress is predictable, normally on the first syllable of the stem, and vowel length varies with stress and the following consonants.

vnotes: Source ambiguous: Yadav frames placement by syllable count and word class with a hedged penultimate 'general pattern', and invokes syllable shape only for ultimate-stressed disyllables ('may normally... when the ultimate syllable is either closed... or ends in a sequence of vowels'); whether that makes the system 'weight-hedged' or a 'fixed-dominant' penult with a weight-type exception class is a catalog vocabula
693.dq: Below a preliminary study of the position of primary word stress in Maithili is given.
693.heavy: Yadav: an ultimate syllable that 'is either closed, i.e., ends in a consonant or a cluster of consonants, or ends in a sequence of vowels - which is diphthongized' attracts stress; no general definition of heavy given, vowel length not invoked (transcription contrasts a vs schwa). Hayes 1995 / StressTyp2 (carried): heavy = long vowels.
693.dflt: penultimate (Yadav's 'general pattern'; also Hayes' elsewhere case)
693.prule: Yadav 1996: monosyllables stressed; disyllables mostly penult, but ultimate if the final syllable is closed or ends in a vowel sequence (and in inflected causatives); trisyllables mostly penult, a small number antepenult (['bərhiyã]), a few ultimate ([hosi'yar], [əsən'tokh]); quadrisyllabic nouns/adjectives almost all antepenult ([bəm'reṭiya]) except some borrowings with penult ([əgər'bətti]); quadrisyllabic verbs penult ([pəhũ'caeb]); 'despite a few exceptions, the general pattern is... penultimate'. Hayes 1995 (StressTyp2 carried quote): heavy penult -> penult; else heavy final -> final; else heavy antepenult -> antepenult; else penult.
693.srule: Only in compounds: 'In compound nouns of four syllables, the two components retain their original patterns – the first component having the primary stress and the second the secondary stress' ([ˈcaruˌtərəph], [ˈbunəˌbəla]); no secondary or rhythmic stress is described for simplex words (all simplex examples of 1-4 syllables carry one stress mark).

morph.rootq: Sec. 2.6.1 (pp.46-49) states stress by word class and syllable count from the right edge of the whole word, never relative to the root/stem: 'A great majority of disyllabic nouns, pronouns, adjectives, and verb infinitives receive stress on their penultimate syllable' (p.47) ... 'To sum up, despite a few exceptions, the general pattern is for most words in Maithili to receive stress on the penultimate syllable' (p.49). Morphology enters only as class exceptions, not as a root anchor: 'Inflected causative verb forms, however, receive stress on the ultimate syllable, e.g., [kə'ʈa] cause to cut' (p.47, i.e. the causative suffix is stressed); 'All verbs of four syllables receive stress on the…
morph.elicq: 'Stress in Maithili is far weaker than in English. ... Below a preliminary study of the position of primary word stress in Maithili is given.' (p.46); 'The account of segmental phonology and stress is based rather closely on the author's earlier works on Maithili phonetics and phonology — in particular Yadav (1976) and chapter two of Yadav (1984d).' (p.20). No elicitation method is stated; all supporting data are isolated citation forms in phonetic brackets sorted by syllable count (['ədmi] 'man', [bi'lai] 'cat', [kən'pəṭṭi] 'temple', ...). The author (a native speaker) separately published instrumental work — Yadav 1984d ch. V 'Acoustic analysis of word stress' and Yadav 1986 'Acoustic…
morph.stmt: 'To sum up, Maithili is a nominative-accusative rather than an ergative language; it shows SOV, GN, AN, NREL, VAUX, and NPO ordering, and it is a suffixing language.' (p.305); 'the verb phrase in Maithili is overwhelmingly fusional; typically a number of affixes are suffixed to the main verb stem or to the auxiliary verb stem' (p.304); 'Finite verb = stem + tense + mood + person/honorificity agreement' (p.153). No prefixes are described anywhere in the grammar; negation, interrogation, plurality and definiteness of nouns are handled by free particles/words rather than affixes.

694.heavy: a long first vowel (Jacobsen/Davidson); Werle 2010: long vowels are moraic in the southern languages; in Makah coda glides 'are consonants, not contributing to syllable weight', and coda nasals count only in Nuu-chah-nulth, so Makah heavy = long vowel only
694.dflt: peninitial (second syllable; #LL -> LĹ, iambic per Werle 2010)
694.prule: Accent on the first syllable if its vowel is long; if the first vowel is short, accent on the second syllable (Jacobsen 1979b:4, endorsed by Davidson 2002 n.10 'This rule correctly places primary accent in Makah'). Werle 2010:16 adds that 'consistent peninitial stress for some Makah speakers (Jacobsen 1979b)' is also reported, i.e. a quantity-insensitive second-syllable pattern for a subset of speakers.
694.srule: Possible but not established; no placement given: 'there may be secondary accent at work as well since there are sometimes perceived prominences in addition to the primary accent, especially on long vowels. It is unclear whether these are merely phonetic correlates of vowel length or part of the accent system' (Davidson 2002: 350 n.10). Not mentioned for Makah in Werle 2002 (sec. 2.1, single initial foot) or Werle 2010 (sec. 4.2); Wilson 1986: 290 had stated that Nootkan 'lost secondary stress'.

morph.rootq: Davidson 2002 §2.5 p.24-25: 'accent placement in Nuuchahnulth is governed by a rather different rule from that found in Makah, formulated by Jacobsen (1979b: 4) as follows: “If the first vowel of a word is long, the accent falls on this syllable; if it is short, the accent falls on the second syllable.”' Endnote 10: 'This rule correctly places primary accent in Makah, but there may be secondary accent at work as well since there are sometimes perceived prominences in addition to the primary accent, especially on long vowels. ... Accent in Makah is stress accent'. The rule is stated over the word (first two syllables), with no reference to root or stem; Werle 2010:16 likewise: 'Ditidaht and…
morph.elicq: No statement of how Makah accent was observed: Davidson simply quotes the rule from Jacobsen's pedagogical primer (1979b:4) and adds (endnote 10) 'there are sometimes perceived prominences in addition to the primary accent, especially on long vowels. It is unclear whether these are merely phonetic correlates of vowel length or part of the accent system.' His own Nuuchahnulth accent check is text-based ('Sapir (1924) ... This text is too short (284 word tokens) for a complete analysis', §2.5), but nothing comparable is said for Makah; the Makah corpus in general is 'my own elicitation notes and texts that I have collected (primarily from speaker HW)' (§1.3 p.5).
morph.stmt: Davidson 2002 §4.2 p.92: 'Makah and Nuuchahnulth are polysynthetic languages making extensive use of suffixation, including enclisis. Reduplicative prefixation, used to form plurals and express aspectual distinctions, is also important. These are the only morphological techniques, apart from a few plural infixes and some aspectually significant changes in vowel length.... There is no prefixation (apart from reduplicative prefixes), compounding, or noun incorporation.' Word = root + lexical suffixes + aspect suffix, followed by an ordered enclitic string =DIM=TEMP=CAUS=POSS=PINV=TENSE=MOOD=PRO=HAB=3PL=RESP=again (§7.5 (483)).

695.dq: The basic facts of word stress in Malayalam are: ... Malayalam is not a tone language. However, it is necessary to distinguish between word level intonation and phrase level intonation in Malayalam.
695.dloc: ch.2, sec. 2.1.3 'Stress and Tone', 2.1.3.1 'Preliminary Facts', p.55 (diss. pagination), statements (46a-b), exx. (47)-(49), tone facts (50)
695.heavy: long vowel (a syllable with 'a long one [vowel]' vs 'a short vowel'); closed syllables/codas play no role in the statement; secondary stress likewise 'on all the remaining long vowels'
695.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable, except that if the first syllable has a short vowel and the second syllable a long vowel, primary stress falls on the second syllable.
695.srule: Secondary stress on all the remaining long vowels, i.e. every long-vowel syllable other than the primary-stressed one (evidence: these syllables carry high tone); words with no further long vowels have no secondary stress, and the word-final high tone is not a secondary stress (ch.2 fn.7).
695.quote: The basic facts of word stress in Malayalam are: (46) a. If the first syllable of a word has a short vowel and the second syllable a long one, the primary stress falls on the second syllable; in all other cases, primary stress is on the first syllable. b. Secondary stress (the evidence for which is the appearance of a high tone. Discussed below.) falls on all the remaining long vowels. Given below are a few examples: (47) a. waraám 'will come' b. wáram 'boon' c. wáaram 'week' d. wáaraam 'will gather' (48) a. paráati 'complaint' b. páaDaayanam 'reading' c. máratakam 'emerald' ... Malayalam is …
695.loc: ch.2, sec. 2.1.3 'Stress and Tone', 2.1.3.1 'Preliminary Facts', p.55 (diss. pagination), statements (46a-b), exx. (47)-(49), tone facts (50)
695.idn: Malayalam (no dialect, region or register specified in the sections read)
695.exq_: A subcompound with a single primary stress and a single word melody acts as a unit, irrespective of the number of stems in it, while each stem in a cocompound is a separate unit, with stress and tone assignment taking place on every stem ... [p.59] Note that the inflectional ending maaṟ does not re…
695.tone: Mohanan (1982:55-56, fn.7 p.105): 'Malayalam is not a tone language', but word-level intonation is distinguished from phrase-level intonation: the word melody is L*H, with a low tone on the primary-stressed syllable and high tones on the word-final syllable and on all secondary-stressed (long-vowel) syllables; secondary stress is diagnosed by this high tone, and the tone-bearing unit is the foot ('characteristic of intonational phenomena, as opposed to tonal phenomena').

morph.rootq: Mohanan 1982 §2.1.3.1 p.55, (46): 'a. If the first syllable of a word has a short vowel and the second syllable a long one, the primary stress falls on the second syllable; in all other cases, primary stress is on the first syllable. b. Secondary stress (the evidence for which is the appearance of a high tone. Discussed below.) falls on all the remaining long vowels.' The rule is stated over the word, not the root: suffixed forms carry one word melody (fn.9 p.105: kuṭṭi 'child', kuṭṭiye 'child-acc.', kuṭṭiyuṭe 'child-gen.' all LH), and the only morphological reference is to compounding -- 'each stem in a cocompound is a separate unit…

695.cfw: Mohanan (1982, 1986) described Malayalam stress as initial except that it moves to a long second syllable after a short first one, a rule adopted by Asher & Kumari (1997) and Hayes (1995), but Terzenbach's (2011) duration measurements and listener tests found no such shift, and Namboodiripad & Garellek (2017) conclude that whether Malayalam has lexical stress at all, and what governs its position, is still undetermined.

696.dq: There are very clear general rules concerning the position of main stress in the Kristang word ... [section 7] Many verbs ... display a tendency to shift their stress from ultimate syllable to penultimate syllable when they are followed by a stressed syllable in the next word. This is particularly so in rapid speech.
696.dloc: Baxter & de Silva 2004, Introduction section 4 'Indication of stressed syllables', p. xii; section 5 'General rules for the placement of stress in the Kristang word', p. xiii (with fn.23-24 at the foot of p. xiii); section 7 'Words shifting stress in the clause', pp. xiv-xv; Baxter 1988 p.220 ('tonic stress is generally on the penultimate syllable') and section 2.3.1 pp.29-30 (stress levels; the 1-0 / 2-1 / 2-0-1-0 display is on p.29).
696.heavy: A word-final syllable closed by a consonant ('words ending in a consonant') attracts stress to the final syllable; words ending in a vowel take penultimate stress. No vowel length in the language; weight is stated only for the final syllable and only as consonant-final vs vowel-final.
696.prule: Rule A: words ending in a vowel are stressed on the penultimate syllable; Rule B: words ending in a consonant are stressed on the final syllable. Exceptions: a large class of verbs with a stressed final open vowel (kumí 'eat', bebé 'drink'; but podi penult), some vowel-final words with antepenultimate stress (família, ánimu), some consonant-final words with non-final stress (ókel, nóbas). Stressed syllabic nasals possible (ńgka 'no').
696.srule: A single secondary stress falls on the first of the two syllables before the primary stress, or on the only syllable before it; syllables after the primary are unstressed; one primary stress per word (kaza 'house' 1-0, kaza 'marry' 2-1, oresang 2-0-1, mintira 2-1-0, kazamintu 2-0-1-0). No weight condition and no further iteration stated.
696.quote: In Kristang most polysyllablic words fall into two large classes according to the position of stress in the word. These classes follow two stress rules: Stress Rule A. Most words which end in a vowel are stressed on the penultimate syllable, as in kaza (= ka + za) 'house' ... kumeria (= ku + me + ri + a) 'food' ... Stress Rule B. Most words ending in a consonant are stressed on the final syllable, as in landes (= lan + des) 'Dutch', natal (= na + tal) 'Christmas'. Nevertheless, stress is not completely predictable in Kristang as there are certain words which are exceptions to the above two ru…

morph.elicq: No statement of how stress judgments were obtained. Context: thesis ch.2 intro (p.35): 'Bearing in mind the limitations of distinctive features for describing sounds (Ladefoged 1980) and the fact that an extensive acoustic and articulatory study of Kristang has not been conducted, I shall adopt the features of Chomsky and Halle (1968)'; §2.3.1 (thesis p.50 = 1988 p.29): 'Regardless of the phonetic nature of stress, in Kristang stressed and unstressed syllables are readily perceivable.'; data statement (1988 p.ix): 'The corpus comprises approximately 25 hours of text transcribed from tape recordings and material transcribed directly from informants. morph.stmt: Kristang is essentially isolating: 'The verb does not show number and is modified for tense, aspect and mood by preverbal particles: TMA particles' (Baxter 1988 p.221); 'Negation of the predicate is performed by means of the NEG category which occurs before TMA and Modals' with four free negators ńgka, nadi, nenáng, nang (pp.137-138); nominal categories are carried by free prenominal articles, relators (ku, sa, di, na, padi) and reduplication ('Reduplication is a feature of the noun class (as it is of the verb, adjective, and adverb classes)', p.220), with 'Compounding... a productive process for the derivation of nouns' (p.100). No productive prefixes or suffixes are described anywhere…

tn.quote: PRCs divide into two groups as far as suprasegmentals are concerned according to whether they developed tone systems or remained stress languages like the lexifier. ... Upper Guinea PRCs ... and Asian PRCs to the second. ... Indo-Portuguese, Sri-Lankan Portuguese, Papiá Kristang, and Batavia Creole always were in contact with Indo-Aryan, Dravidian and Austronesian languages where tone plays no grammatical role. 697.dq: Primary stress occurs on the rightmost stressed syllable of a word in pre-pausal position. This fact is stated as the Main Stress Rule (12). (A rule of Stress Shift, formulated in 4.7, is applicable in non-final forms.) ... In an appropriate stress phrase, main stress may be retracted across a word boundary
697.dloc: LeSourd 1988, sec. 4.1 p. 144: Main Stress Rule (12) and the parenthesis on Stress Shift; sec. 4.7 'Stress Shift' pp. 278-279: 'In an appropriate stress phrase, main stress may be retracted across a word boundary'.
697.heavy: No syllable-weight criterion in the CVV/CVC sense: closed and open syllables count alike and vowel length is derived/predictable (LeSourd 3.3; Olson 2018:10 'This stress pattern is quantity insensitive, so that both open and closed syllables behave identically with respect to stress'). The only distinction the stress rules see is stressable vowels (full vowels i e a o, plus schwa in certain cluster environments or in even-numbered position in a run of schwas) versus unstressable vowels (schwa, some short i before y, and some lexically marked underlying vowels), which are invisible to (skipped by) the syllable count, not merely light. Hayes 1995:215-216 reanalyses this as QS iambs with full vowels bimoraic and CVC light, which is what StressTyp codes.
697.dflt: not applicable as a heavy/light default; every word has stressable vowels; main stress = penultimate stressable vowel (surface penult, or antepenult/earlier when final-region schwas are unstressable)
697.prule: Main Stress Rule: primary stress on the rightmost stressed syllable of the word (pre-pausal), i.e. on the penultimate stressable vowel as placed by the Alternating Stress Rule (stress even-numbered syllables counting right-to-left over stressable vowels only); words with lexically/morphologically specified final stress shift the whole pattern one syllable left.
697.srule: All non-rightmost stresses assigned by LeSourd's rules are secondary: the word-initial syllable (Initial Stress Rule) and every other stressable vowel counting leftward from the primary-stressed penult of the count (Alternating Stress Rule), unstressable vowels (mostly schwa) skipped; an initial clash may optionally be resolved by Clash Avoidance. (Olson 2018 ms.: initial stress rarely realized in modern PMDP dictionary recordings; penult-anchored alternation retained.)

Certain occurrences of /ə/ are inherently stressable: they are available to the stress rules even in environments in which other schwas would be invisible. [4.2.5, p. 177] ... In later chapters, I will argue that some und…
697.tone: Pitch-accent contrasts ride on the stress system (LeSourd 3.5 p. 119; ch. 10 p. 792): 'Both the location of the stressed syllables in a word and the pitch or pitch contour associated with stressed syllables in certain positions in the word are distinctive in Passamaquoddy.' Acute accent = relatively high-pitched stressed syllable; grave = relatively low-pitched stressed syllable (apart from vocatives only on the rightmost stressed syllable, rising before pause); circumflex = distinctively low-pitched final unstressed syllable in certain 3PASS forms. Contrasts mostly distinguish inflected forms; lexical pairs rare. Ch. 10: 'The pitch accent system of Passamaquoddy is one of the most interesting areas in the phonology of the language, but one that remains largely unexplored' -- low pitch on the last stressed syllable arises through Final Vowel Deletion and inherently stressed/pre-stressing final affixes (after Goddard 1970). Stress placement itself is rule-governed (ch. 4), so the stress rules decide the kind.

morph.rootq: "(1) Initial Stress Rule (ISR): Stress the first syllable of a word. (2) Alternating Stress Rule (ASR): Stress the even-numbered syllables of a word, counting from right to left." (p.133); "Primary stress occurs on the rightmost stressed syllable of a word in pre-pausal position." (Main Stress Rule, p.144); "the domain of stress is sometimes larger than the word. In particular, a preverb or prenoun may form a single stress domain with the word it modifies" (p.147). The rules count (stressable) syllables of the whole word/stress phrase, affixes included (e.g. was-is vs. was-is-ək, p.140: 'the stress of non-initial syllables varies with the addition of suffixes'); no reference to root or stem.
morph.elicq: Data: "The principal source of the Passamaquoddy data discussed in this work is my own field notes, collected at Indian Township and at Pleasant Point" (p.7). Both pre-pausal (citation) and connected-speech forms are described: "When a word is final in an utterance, its rightmost stressed syllable is its most prominent syllable. ... When a word or longer stress phrase is followed by other material in connected speech, however, the penultimate stressed syllable (penultimate foot) is the most prominent." (§4.7 Stress Shift, p.278). Also: "Phrase and sentence level stress and intonation are largely ignored in this work" (p.130). No instrumental measurements.
morph.stmt: "The parts of speech in Passamaquoddy are noun, verb, and particle. Both nouns and verbs are highly inflected, largely by suffixation. Verb forms with as many as seven inflectional suffixes are not uncommon." (LeSourd 1988: 14); the only prefixes are the three personal prefixes n(t)-, k(t)-, w(t)- (used in possessed nouns and Independent-order verbs; 'No prefixes are used' in the Conjunct and Imperative orders, p.52), with stems built as Initial(root)-(Medial)-Final.

The grave accent (`) indicates a relatively low-pitched stressed syllable, except that word-final syllables which bear this accent are pronounced with a rising intonation before a pause. The circumflex accent (ˆ) indicates a distinctively low-pitched final unstressed syllable.

697.cfw: LeSourd's 1988 MIT dissertation (published 1993), the standard phonology of Passamaquoddy accent, gives initial stress plus right-to-left alternating stress from the penult counted over full vowels only, with primary stress rightmost, and Olson's 2018 instrumental study of dictionary recordings keeps the same penult-anchored, quantity-insensitive alternation and rightmost primary stress but finds no obligatory initial stress in her speakers, a secondary-stress difference she attributes to a possible speaker-group or generational split.

698.heavy: Galea/Vella: heavy = short vowel + coda consonant (including the first half of a geminate) OR long vowel/diphthong; coda (word-final) consonant extrametrical, so a final syllable attracts stress only if V:C or VCC (superheavy). Sutcliffe: final syllable accented when its vowel is long, or short and followed by two consonants.
698.dflt: penultimate (Sutcliffe: 'In other cases the accent falls on the penultimate syllable')
698.prule: Accent on the final syllable if it has a long vowel or a short vowel followed by two consonants (i.e. superheavy once the final consonant is extrametrical); otherwise on the penultimate; never earlier than the penult in native words (Sutcliffe 1936). Galea 2016/Vella 1995 restate this as stress on the rightmost heavy syllable (moraic trochees, final-consonant extrametricality), e.g. [ˈnɪk.tbʊ], [nɪˈsɪlfʊ], /ˈsɐffɐr/.

698.cfw: Vella's own rule in Grice, Vella and Bruggeman 2019, the Brame rule as restated in Wolf 2012/2016, Galea 2016 with its transcribed forms, and Sutcliffe 1936 all put Maltese stress on the rightmost heavy syllable, with superheavy finals and heavy penults stressed and plain closed finals skipped, differing only in how they phrase the default for words with no heavy syllable, which Wolf notes makes no difference at the surface.

evidence_works.detail: A theoretical (non-instrumental) analysis of Standard Maltese phonology that rejects the Brame-style cyclic stress-plus-syncope account and states word stress as a single post-lexical rule: penultimate unless the final syllable ends in a consonant cluster or a long vowel plus consonant, in which case final; the rightmost stressed vowel surfaces long. It adds the exceptions: Romance/English loans with antepenultimate stress (pubbliku, muzika ~ muzika variants, fertili doublets) and lexically marked final-stressed loans (virtu, kafe), so it supplies the weight rule the catalog entry leaves blank

evidence_works.work: Grice & Anna Bruggeman 2019, Stress, pitch accent, and beyond: Intonation in Maltese questions (Journal of Phonetics 76: 100913 (pp. 1-17). doi:10.1016/j.wocn.2019.100913)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article restates the weight-based Maltese stress rule (rightmost heavy syllable within the last three, closed final syllable only if superheavy, default penult) and then shows that in direct questions the main pitch peak sits at the left edge of the question word rather than on its stressed syllable, while in declaratives the fall is completed over the stressed syllable (H*+L pitch accent). Stressed-vowel duration was found to be 'rather constant, and generally unaffected by rising/falling intonational events occurring on the word' (p. 11), so the only durational effects were phrase-final

699.heavy: bimoraic rhyme: syllables with a coda consonant (VC, VCC, incl. glottal/nasal codas) and syllables with a branching nucleus (diphthongs VV; also contrastive long vowels e.g. /aat/ 'big'); onsets weightless; superheavy (VVC, VVCC) not distinguished from heavy; post-lexical stressed-vowel lengthening does not count
699.dflt: final syllable of the root (End Rule [Final])
699.prule: Domain = root (stratum 1). Quantity Sensitivity: every heavy syllable in the root receives foot-level stress; End Rule [Final, Word] places primary stress on the rightmost of these. If the root has no heavy syllable, End Rule [Final, Foot] stresses the rightmost (light) syllable of the root, which then carries primary stress. Outer suffix strata (person/tense/mood) are never stressed even when heavy.
699.srule: Secondary (foot-level) stress on every heavy (CVC/CVV) syllable of the root other than the rightmost, which carries primary stress; outside the root only secondary stress occurs, and only on heavy syllables of the affix classes closest to the root (oblique/object markers, auxiliary suffixes, manner suffixes, noun classifiers, temporal modifiers); the outermost affixes (subject, tense/evidentiality, mood, final nominal suffixes) are never stressed even when heavy. Weight-driven, not rhythmic: 'there is no pattern of alternating stress'.

699.exq_: The true exceptions, then, are those nouns with /-i/ final syllables which have no semantic content. These final /i/ vowels function simply as markers of an ‘/i/ class’ of noun roots that are defined morphologically as having an unaccentuable final syllable. [likewise /a/-class verb roots, p.187]
699.tone: Mamaindê is a tone language (contrastive lexical tone; four tone patterns) that also has stress; pitch is not a correlate of stress (correlates are length, vowel quality, amplitude) and tone cannot be used to predict stress: stressed syllables can carry any of the four tone patterns (Eberhard 2009: 141, 190-191).

tn.quote: Mamaindê is a tone language that also has stress. … Here I posit a tone system for Mamaindê comprised of only 2 underlying tones, H and L.174 These two tones can then be combined into a total of 4 surface patterns when spread over any bi-moraic syllable: H, L, L-H and H-L.175 This differs from Kingston's analysis where he posits 4 contrastive tones - two register tones, H and L, and two contour tones, Rising and Falling … Contour tones on syllables will be shown to follow from the fact that in Mamaindê tones (H or L) are lexically associated to moras, instead of syllables.
tn.cite: Eberhard, David M. 2009. Mamaindê Grammar: A Northern Nambikwara language and its cultural context. PhD dissertation, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Utrecht: LOT (LOT Dissertation Series 236).
tn.locator: sect. 2.4.2 'Stress vs. Tone', p. 190 (first sentence); sect. 2.4.4.1 'Underlying Tones', p. 198 (rest)
tn.note: Two underlying tones, H and L, one per mora; heavy syllables may carry HL or LH (four surface patterns); a floating L marks the negative; tone is independent of the weight-based word stress.

700.dq: Stress is not phonemic in Mam. Every word has one stress, according to the following rules ... Words have one and only one stress and have no more than one long vowel. Therefore juncture must occur somewhere between two stresses or two long vowels in a segment.
700.dloc: England 1975 section 1.3 'Stress', pp. 35-36; section 1.2.4 'Juncture', p. 33; section 1.2.3 'Glottal stop', p. 33 (England 1983:37 carried via StressTyp2 entry)
700.heavy: Heaviest: a long vowel (a word has at most one, and it always takes the stress). Next: a vowel followed by glottal stop (V7 / Vʔ), the LAST such vowel in the word winning; England treats the glottal stop as a vowel feature, and states that other (coda) consonants do not have this effect. No other closed syllable counts as heavy; the fallback is the vowel preceding the last consonant of the root/stem (a morphologically anchored default), which Hayes 1995/StressTyp2 reinterpret as a third tier 'VC#'.
700.dflt: the vowel preceding the last consonant of the root (1975) / stem (1983), i.e. the root-final syllable nucleus; suffixes and enclitics without a long vowel or glottal stop are skipped (e.g. /b'ala/ 'maybe' with enclitic -la stressed on the root vowel, giving a surface penult).
700.prule: Exactly one stress per word: (1) on the long vowel if the word has one; (2) else on the vowel preceding the last glottal stop in the word; (3) else on the vowel preceding the last consonant of the root (1983: stem), so suffixes/enclitics lacking V: or ʔ are never stressed; (4) a root with a single vowel stresses that vowel.
700.srule: None: 'Every word has one stress' (1.3, p. 35); 'Words have one and only one stress' (1.2.4, p. 33). Confirmed for Northern (Todos Santos) Mam by Elkins & Kuo 2023:1 'There is no secondary stress.'

700.loc: England 1975 section 1.3 'Stress', pp. 35-36; section 1.2.4 'Juncture', p. 33; section 1.2.3 'Glottal stop', p. 33 (England 1983:37 carried via StressTyp2 entry)
700.idn: England 1975 describes the Mam of San Ildefonso Ixtahuacan, Huehuetenango, 'where a dialect of Northern Mam is spoken' (Introduction); the weight-conditioned rule is stated for that Northern Mam variety. (England 1983, the record's corroborating cite, is the same author's grammar; it was not consulted again.)

morph.rootq: §1.3 STRESS, p.35: "Stress is not phonemic in Mam. Every word has one stress, according to the following rules: 1. Stress falls on a long vowel in the word. 2. If there is no long vowel, stress falls on the vowel preceding the last glottal stop in the word. 3. If there is no long vowel and no glottal stop, stress falls on the vowel preceding the last consonant in the root. 4. If none of the above conditions apply, stress falls on the only vowel in the root. That is, stress is conditioned by long vowels and glottal stop and never falls on suffixes unless they contain long vowels or glottal stop." (example p.36: [ɓa'lə] /b'ala/ 'maybe' ({-la} is an enclitic)).
morph.elicq: The stress section (§1.3, p.35-36) gives rules and six example words with no statement of how stress was observed. The only evidential remarks are general: §0.2 p.10 "The data used for this analysis consist of a Mam-Spanish dictionary compiled by the Mam students at the PLFM, a substantial body of texts and dialogues collected and transcribed by the author and the Mam students and analyzed by the author, ... and various materials elicited directly by the author."; and §1.2.4 p.34 (juncture): "Pause can occur after directionals, and they can also receive stress, although in connected speech they usually do not."
morph.stmt: England (p.34, 42): "Morphemes consist of prefixes, roots, suffixes, or enclitics. Clitics are almost always postposed to the word... (the only exception seems to be qa 'plural' which can be preposed to the word)"; "Affixes consist of both prefixes and suffixes, and are inflectional or derivational" -- concretely, person (Set A/Set B) and aspect inflection is prefixal/preposed (verb template p.35: 'unbound aspect # Set B + Directional # Set A + Stem + Enclitics'), while mode (-al/-a7/-m) and virtually all of the 84 derivational affixes (§2.4; the only prefixes are s-/xh-/x-/ch- #1 and aj- #48-49) are suffixes, with person and sentence-level enclitics following.

tn.quote: As was initially noted for Ixtahuacán Mam by England (1983b, p. 35), there is a distinct pitch difference between certain vowels which are followed by glottal stops and vowels which are not … In Todos Santos Mam … it is only word-medially that Vʔ sequences are realized with falling pitch, without glottal stricture. … This contrast between flat and falling pitch is obligatory … despite carrying a very low functional load: … in no word does pitch/glottalization alone contrast meaning. … the system we see today is simply an incipient tonal contrast. … (Mam does not have contrastive tone).
tn.cite: Elkins, Noah Eli. 2023. The interplay of syntax and prosody in Mam. PhD dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles.
tn.locator: ch. 2 sec. 2.2 'Incipient tone', pp. 69-71, and Part II ch. 3 sec. 3.2.1 'Downstep and pitch reset', p. 221
tn.note: No contrastive tone. A vowel before word-medial glottal stop surfaces with falling pitch: an incipient tonal contrast with no minimal pairs. Other pitch is intonational, on the stressed syllable.

701.dq: There is one general condition on primary stress position in Manam: no primary stress can be farther from the end of a word than its antepenultimate syllable. ... The rightmost stress in a word is primary ...; all the other stresses are secondary
701.dloc: Ch. 2, section 2.7 'Stress' and 2.7.1 'Primary stress', book pp. 50-56 (Rules 17-20 and the suffix rule); lexically marked stress pp. 56-57; 2.7.3 'Secondary stress' pp. 63-65 (Rules 25-27); syllable structure (C)V(N), section 2.4 pp. 21-22
701.heavy: closed syllables -- at the phonemic level the syllable is (C)V(N), so 'closed' = nasal-coda (Rule 17 V -> [+1stress]/_N(C(w))...); these attract primary (and secondary, Rule 25) stress. No long vowels: 'in vowel sequences, each vowel belongs to a separate syllable'; but a penult vowel immediately preceded by a tautomorphemic vowel sends stress to the antepenult (Rule 18: móasi, góai).
701.dflt: penultimate (antepenultimate when the penult vowel is immediately preceded by a tautomorphemic vowel, or before the listed word-final object/adnominal suffixes)
701.prule: Three-syllable right window ('no primary stress can be farther from the end of a word than its antepenultimate syllable'). Default penult (Rule 19). A closed (nasal-final) syllable in final, penult, or antepenult position takes primary stress (Rule 17; an antepenult closed syllable only if no morpheme boundary follows it and the word is not an intransitive verb, else penult). If the penult vowel is immediately preceded by another vowel with no intervening morpheme boundary, stress is antepenultimate (Rule 18). Monosyllables stressed (Rule 20). Certain word-final suffixes (1sg/3sg/3pl object, 3sg/3pl adnominal, etc.) require antepenultimate stress unless the penult is closed, in which case the penult is stressed. Four lexemes (sará, sarará, bourá, bouŋʔurá) and monosyllabic intransitive verb roots carry lexically marked stress.
701.srule: Secondary stress (purely phonological): the rightmost stress is primary, all others secondary. Rule 27 puts secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward from the primary (tanèpwa-tína, tìna-dì-a-rú-a-lo); Rule 25 puts it on a nasal-closed syllable one to three syllables before a stress (mòmbwa-tína, i-dàn-dàn-la-lá?o) and Rule 26 on the first vowel of a tautomorphemic VV sequence (gòai-tína, di-sòa?i-nó?a), both taking precedence over Rule 27; adjacent stresses are allowed; stresses weaken progressively leftward.

702.dq: The present analysis agrees with the fact that in Mandarin, both heavy-heavy and heavy-light disyllables are common, but light-heavy and light-light disyllables are not found ... Let us now consider stress in compounds and phrases. ... assume that stress is determined by syntactic relation. Specifically, a syntactic nonhead should have more stress than a syntactic head.
702.dloc: Duanmu 2000 ms. sec. 4.1 (pp. 4-6) and sec. 4.4 (pp. 13-14); Duanmu 2011 sec. 3, exx. (5)-(7); Chao 1968:35,38 as carried by Duanmu
702.heavy: Heavy = 'full' syllable with a VX rime (VC, diphthong VG, or long vowel; bimoraic), which carries a lexical tone; light = 'weak' syllable with reduced V rime (coda dropped / vowel shortened, ~50% rime duration), toneless (neutral tone). 'In Mandarin, all full syllables are heavy'; Weight-Stress Principle: stressed syllables are heavy, light syllables are unstressed.
702.dflt: not applicable (light-light and light-heavy disyllables 'are not found'; every word contains a full syllable)
702.prule: Every full (heavy, tone-bearing) syllable is stressed and forms its own bimoraic foot; weak (light, toneless) syllables are unstressed; which syllables are weak is a lexical property of the morpheme/word (StressTyp2: 'determined lexically'). Relative prominence among full syllables is barely perceptible and disputed: Chao 1968:35 says the last full syllable is strongest ('medium-light-heavy'), Duanmu analyses disyllabic feet as left-headed (trochaic) and compound/phrase prominence as syntactic (Nonhead Stress).
702.srule: Degrees of stress in Duanmu's analysis: every full (heavy, tone-bearing) syllable is stressed as the head of its own bimoraic M-foot, so full syllables that do not head a disyllabic S-foot still carry a lower degree of stress, and weak (light, toneless) syllables carry none; S-feet are disyllabic and left-headed, pairing syllables from the left in polysyllabic names (ex. (13) (jee-luu)-(saa-leN) 'Jerusalem': S-foot heads on syllables 1 and 3), with main stress on the initial syllable (made explicit in Duanmu 2004: 69-70, 96: 'three degrees of stress'); prominence among feet in compounds/phrases follows Nonhead Stress. The author notes that distinctions among full syllables are barely perceptible to speakers.
702.quote: It is well-known that stress in Chinese is hard to feel. ... Chao (1968: 35) suggests that in a string of full syllables, the last has most stress, the first has slightly less, and the rest have still less. This is known as the ‘medium-light-heavy’ theory. However, as Chao (1968: 38) acknowledges, Mandarin speakers do not agree on where stress is, therefore the medium-light-heavy theory is hard to confirm. ... In dialects like Mandarin, there is a difference between full syllables, such as le4 ‘happy,’ and weak syllables, such as the aspect marker le (which indicates completion). Full syllabl…
702.loc: Duanmu 2000 ms. sec. 4.1 (pp. 4-6) and sec. 4.4 (pp. 13-14); Duanmu 2011 sec. 3, exx. (5)-(7); Chao 1968:35,38 as carried by Duanmu

702.exq_: Full syllables are longer and carry tone. Weak syllables are shorter and usually do not carry tone. ... In Mandarin, weak syllables are unstressed and do not carry an underlying tone. 702.tone: Tone language: full syllables bear one of four lexical tones; weak (neutral-tone) syllables are toneless and a de-stressed full syllable loses its tone ('Since Chinese is a tone language, F0 contour cannot be freely used to indicate stress', Duanmu 2000 sec. 4.2; Tone-Stress Principle, Duanmu 2011).

evidence_works.note: Describes Kunming hua (Southwestern Mandarin, under mand1415), not Beijing/Standard Mandarin (PTH), which it contrasts throughout. Data 'from native Kunming people' following 'the most conservative path' (p. 2), with the 头 suffix examples taken from Gui 1990 and re-transcribed (fn. 7). Adds that the unstressed (neutral-tone) syllable in Kunming has a constant mid-level 33 pitch ('Unlike PTH the neutral tone in KMH consistently has the pitch value of mid-level (i.e. 33)', sec. 3.3, printed p. 25), at the same morphological loci as in PTH (reduplicated kin terms, suffixes 头/首, particle 了), and that 头 keeps its tone when stressed with its full meaning 'head' (p. 26). No statement on stress placement among full syllables. The citation-tone values (printed p. 20) are said to rest on 'our own acoustical studies', with no procedure, instrument or numbers given; the neutral-tone section (pp. 25-26) reports no measurement.

702.cfw: Duanmu 1990 and 2000, Dell 2004, Fon 2002, Huang 2004 and Yu and colleagues 2024 all treat Mandarin stress as lexical (which syllables are weak, neutral-toned, is fixed word by word, with no set position of main stress), while Dell 2004 rejects Duanmu's initial-prominent feet in favour of the right-edge prominence reported by Chao 1968 and Hoa 1983, so the position of stress among full syllables stays unsettled.

703.heavy: Closed syllable only: trisyllabic roots are penult-stressed 'expecially if this syllable is closed'; initial-stressed trisyllabic roots 'generally have open penultimate syllable, but exceptions to this are found'. Vowel length is not mentioned as a weight factor in the reachable text.
703.dflt: penultimate remains the stated norm; in trisyllabic roots with an open penult stress is often initial (=antepenult), not categorically
703.prule: Penultimate stress norm: almost all bisyllabic words are penult(=initial)-stressed regardless of constituency; the general tendency is penultimate word-syllable stress. Trisyllabic unreduplicated nominal roots are 'predominantly' penultimate, especially when the penult is closed; 'many' roots have initial stress instead (these generally have an open penult, with exceptions), and a few vary between initial and penult. Stress also shifts with inflection/derivation (syllable structure of the resulting form; sec. 3.5.1.1).
703.srule: Three stress levels are recognised (primary, secondary, tertiary/unstressed; 3.3.2.3). Quadrisyllabic unreduplicated nominal roots, pattern 1: primary and secondary stresses on the penultimate and first syllables (wáridila, wúrumūmu, gálijūru, wánudùwa; frozen reduplicated roots báragbarag, jaguyágu follow this pattern); which of the two is the primary is not securely recoverable from the held excerpt (Goedemans 2010: 677 'often unclear which is primary'). Pattern-2 roots (major stress on the antepenult) show only 'decay of intensity in the following two syllables'. Nominal roots of more than four syllables: a secondary stress on the penultimate syllable (yinjinjimani 'goanna tail'). No alternating rhythm is described; bi- and trisyllabic words carry one stress.

704.dq: Bij twee- of meerlettergrepige grondwoorden valt de klemtoon, ofschoon zwak, op de voorlaatste lettergreep. ... De klemtoon verspringt niet, ook al worden er achtervoegsels of nadrukwoorden aan het grondwoord gehecht. (p. 23 §10a; sentence emphasis is treated separately in §83 p. 84: 'Willen wij nadruk op een woord leggen, dan doen we dit gewoonlijk door een sterkere klemtoon op het betreffende w…
704.dloc: Burger 1946: 23, 'Klemtoon' §10a (stress) and 'Woordvorm' §11 (only the final syllable can be closed) (the Internet Archive 20200211151026); compound/particle-group stress §30a p. 36; sentence emphasis §83 p. 84.
704.heavy: A penult with a full (non-pepet) vowel bears stress; a penult whose vowel is pepet (schwa) rejects stress to the final syllable. Vowel length and syllable closure are not the criterion: §11 states that only the word-final syllable can be closed, never the penult (homorganic nasal+stop counts as one sound). Burger adds that before voiceless consonants stress 'soms' (sometimes) stays on the pepet anyway, especially in proper names; the ST1 'prenasalisation as coda' idea is the database coder's hypothesis, not Burger's.
704.dflt: Not decided by the source: with two pepets 'is het dikwijls moeilijk uit te maken, welke meer betoond wordt' (often hard to tell which is more stressed).
704.prule: Stress ('though weak') on the penultimate syllable of di- and polysyllabic base words (semàmboe, djàrang); if the penult contains a pepet (schwa), stress falls on the final syllable (remàng). Stress does not shift when suffixes or emphatic words are attached to the base (àména 'his father' < amé; ìtoekali < kali), so affixed words can surface with antepenultimate stress. Before voiceless consonants stress sometimes stays on the pepet anyway, especially in proper names (Nèkang, Lèmpé); with two pepets it is often hard to tell which is more stressed. Proper names make further exceptions: initial stress in Djoema'ak, Sapatoe, final in Oeloemboe, Empoto (compounds). 'The less we Europeans stress a syllable, the closer we are to the truth.'
704.srule: Only in compounds and word + modal/emphatic-particle groups: these form one stress unit with the main stress on the last member, and Burger notes 'bijtonen' (subsidiary accents) in them that sometimes make the main stress hard to locate; where they fall is not given (§30a p. 36; §206 p. 246 'hoofd- en bijtonen niet altijd gemakkelijk... te onderscheiden'). No secondary stress is described for simple or affixed words (§10a p. 23: one, weak, stress per word). Verheijen & Grimes 1995 §2.3 (p. 588) likewise mention none.

morph.rootq: Burger 1946 sec. 10a, p. 23: 'Bij twee- of meerlettergrepige grondwoorden valt de klemtoon, ofschoon zwak, op de voorlaatste lettergreep. Bevat deze een pepet, dan ligt de klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep. ... De klemtoon verspringt niet, ook al worden er achtervoegsels of nadrukwoorden aan het grondwoord gehecht. àména, zijn vader (amé is vader); ìtoekali (kali is nadrukwoord).' [Stress is stated on the grondwoord (base word) and does not shift when suffixes or enclitic emphatic words are attached.]
morph.elicq: No elicitation method is stated; the description is the author's auditory impression from years of fieldwork (missionary at Ruteng, folk-tale texts). Sec. 10a, p. 23: 'Algemeen kan van de beklemtoning worden gezegd: hoe minder wij, Europeanen, een lettergreep beklemtonen, hoe dichter wij bij het juiste zijn.' Sec. 206, p. 246: 'Het zwakke Mangg. accent laat een Europees oor dikwijls in de steek, omdat hoofd- en bijtonen niet altijd gemakkelijk en zeker te onderscheiden zijn.' (cf. sec. 201, p. 238 on intonation: 'Om tot zekere gegevens te komen, zou men met apparaten moeten werken. Wanneer ik naar Manggaraiers luisterde ...').
morph.stmt: Arka & Kosmas 2005 sec. 2: 'Morphologically, Manggarai is isolating (i.e. words in Manggarai are typically monomorphemic)' and sec. 3: 'Manggarai is poor in verbal morphology and makes use of clitics'; Burger 1946 agrees: no conjugation (sec. 109 'wij hebben hier geen echte vervoeging'), no passive, no number, no article, tenseless verb — the only bound morphology is post-posed: the pronominal/possessive 'achtervoegsels' (enclitics -k, -h, -i/-n, -t, -km, -m, -s, -d, which may land at the end of the word group), words shortened to enclitic suffixes (-t, -m), and one derivational suffix -ng (locative/benefactive/causative/denominal); the only pre-posed bound elements are the proclitic…

secx.sec_quote_tr: In ema koé the main stress lies on koé. But this criterion is only supplementary. For we also have unity of stress with modal or emphatic particles and the word concerned. Maikoé! 'come!', nggitoedéng 'thus'. Moreover, because of the subsidiary accents (bijtonen) it is sometimes difficult to make out where the main stress lies.
secx.primary_revised_quote: Words are stressed on the penultimate syllable of the root. If, however, the penultimate syllable contains a schwa hi that is not followed by a prenasalised stop, then the ultimate syllable is stressed. The addition of enclitics does not effect the stress on the root.

705.heavy: Bimoraic syllable = heavy: long vowel (CV:) or falling/level-sonority diphthong (CVV) (de Lacy); Hyman/StressTyp2 rank them: long vowel ('geminate cluster') outranks diphthong ('non-identical vowel cluster') outranks short vowel. No codas exist in Maori.
705.prule: Main stress on the leftmost syllable with a long vowel; if none, on the leftmost syllable with a diphthong; if none, on the first syllable (Hyman 1977 after Biggs/Hohepa; de Lacy 2003 collapses long V and diphthong as 'bimoraic syllable, else leftmost'). de Lacy adds: only one heavy syllable per root, so the long-vowel-vs-diphthong ranking rarely competes root-internally.
705.srule: None inside the prosodic word: de Lacy's *FT- ('Don’t have a non-head foot (i.e. secondary stress)') leaves one stress per prosodic word; a longer morphological word has one stress per prosodic word because every root, every bimoraic prefix (whaka-), the passive allomorph -tia and each half of a long loan is its own prosodic word, each stressed by the main rule. Earlier descriptions state word-level secondary stresses differently (Hohepa 1967:10: on the next-ranked syllable by the same weight scale; Biggs 1969:133 rule 5: 'on every alternate vowel preceding the heaviest stress'; Bauer 1993:573ff: on every morpheme of two or more morae); Keegan 2023 transcribes ˌke.re.ˈrū ~ ˈke.re.ˌrū, ˈu.a.ˌu.a without a rule.

ev.text: From our observations in the present dataset we are able to formulate a number of preliminary generalisations about word stress in Mawng. Monosyllabic and disyllabic words always have initial stress. For example in both 'marlu' [...] "wind" and 'murlirrk' [...] "shoulder" stress is on the initial syllable. The fact that a heavy syllable in non-initial position does not attract stress suggests that the Mawng stress system is quantity-insensitive[fn. 7: Capell & Hinch (1970:27) suggest that stress assignment is quantity sensitive (being attracted to a heavy antepenult) in words of four or more syllables; their account is however very brief and does not take morphological structure into accoun…

708.dq: Hellmuth et al. 2007: 'An intonational pitch accent is usually associated with the stressed syllable of all content words in the utterance' and 'we are able to formulate a number of preliminary generalisations about word stress in Mawng' (word stress described separately from phrasal pitch accents and boundary tones).
708.dloc: Hellmuth, Kuegler & Singer 2007: first dq sentence in sec. 2.1 'Global intonational contours observed in our data', p. 1; second dq sentence in sec. 2.2.1 'Word-level metrical prominence', p. 6 (section runs pp. 5-7). Cf. Capell & Hinch 1970 ch. 1 sec. 1.5 'Intonation', p. 27 (phonological word ~ grammatical word; publisher text read via Google Books, the 2017 De Gruyter reprint).
708.heavy: Closed syllable (Capell & Hinch via StressTyp2 entry: 'When a closed syllable precedes the penult, it may take stress'; Hellmuth et al. fn. 7: 'heavy antepenult'; their QI counter-example murlirrk treats a closed CVCC syllable as the heavy type). Vowel length is not phonemic in Maung (Capell & Hinch 1970:23 'though length is not phonemic', read in an online text whose provenance we do not cite).
708.dflt: penult in words of four or more syllables (Capell & Hinch); first~second syllable 'equally stressed' in words of up to three syllables (C&H) / initial (Hellmuth et al. 2007)
708.prule: Capell & Hinch 1970:27 (publisher text read): 'Stress is not contrastive and varies freely within certain limits.' Words of up to three syllables: the first two syllables 'tend to be equally stressed' (gumbil 'chest', baladji 'bag'). Words of four or more syllables: stress 'tends to fall on the penultimate' (jiniwunjan, awunilanun), but 'when a closed syllable (CVC, CVCC) precedes the penultimate, it tends to take the primary stress' (jiniwudbunjan, jinimijarmanun). Sec. 1.5 restates: 'The stress is equal on words of three syllables or less and tends to be on the penultimate in longer words.' Hellmuth, Kuegler & Singer 2007 (own data, 'preliminary'): mono-/disyllables always initial; trisyllables first or second syllable (variable within and across speakers, incl. the loan name 'Amanda'); 4+ syllables two stresses, initial and penultimate (of word or root), which is primary varies word to word; in nouns the accent 'almost always falls on the leftmost foot (the first syllable of the root)', prefixed verbs more variable; they read the system as quantity-insensitive and trochaic (fn. 7 disputes C&H's weight clause) and assume initial stress for their alignment study.
708.srule: Capell & Hinch 1970:27: in words of four or more syllables 'additional stresses may fall on alternate preceding syllables' before the penultimate main stress (jiniwunjan, awunilanun), i.e. alternating stresses counted leftward from the penult (hedged 'may'); in words of up to three syllables the first two syllables are 'equally stressed' (no primary/secondary ranking). Hellmuth, Kuegler & Singer 2007: words of 4+ syllables 'tend to have two stresses, on both initial and penultimate syllables (of the word or root)', which is primary varying word to word; whether occasional extra pitch accents on a word are 'rhythmic secondary stress' is left open.
708.quote: [Capell & Hinch 1970:27] Stress is not contrastive and varies freely within certain limits. The first two syllables of words up to three syllables in length tend to be equally stressed, e.g., /gumbil/ 'chest', /baladji/ 'bag'. On words of four syllables or longer stress tends to fall on the penultimate and additional stresses may fall on alternate preceding syllables, e.g., /jiniwunjan/ 'he cooked it', /awunilanun/ 'he was eating them'. However, when a closed syllable (CVC, CVCC) precedes the penultimate, it tends to take the primary stress, e.g., /jiniwudbunjan/ 'he started it (the engine)',…
708.loc: Capell & Hinch 1970 ch. 1 sec. 1.4 'Stress', p. 27 (with the opening of sec. 1.5 'Intonation'); Hellmuth, Kuegler & Singer 2007 sec. 2.2.1, pp. 6-7 incl. footnote 7 on p. 6 (section runs pp. 5-7)
708.idn: Mawng (HKS 2007, Singer 2006) = Maung (Capell & Hinch 1970); no dialects or sub-varieties named; data: C&H 1970: Goulburn Island, North Australia; Capell's fieldwork 1939 and 1942 plus later shorter contacts, Hinch resident at the Methodist Mission, grammar formalised at the 1966 SIL workshop (Brisbane), informant…

711.dq: It has been established earlier that stress in the dialects of Moksha is mainly located on the word-initial syllable. ... On the basis of the present findings it can be suggested that sentence prosody plays a significant role in the realisations of stress within a word. (p. 75)
711.dloc: Ch. 4 Conclusions p. 75; also section 3.2 p. 38 (89% initial in 2457 tokens), Introduction p. 19, Ch. 2 pp. 25-26 (Paasonen 1903: 8 'Der mokschanische accent ist frei'), pp. 29-30 (dialects; 'in no dialect do the two tendencies exclude each other')
711.heavy: Vowel quality, not length or coda: a non-initial syllable with low a (or ä) attracts stress away from an initial syllable containing a high vowel i or u (which may surface as schwa); no phonemic vowel length; closed vs open syllable plays no role in placement (South-Western dialects only: shift said to be blocked by an open word-final syllable, Devayev 1963).
711.prule: Stress mainly on the word-initial syllable; it tends to be located on a subsequent syllable containing low a/ä when the initial syllable has high i/u (Paasonen 1903 tradition; Kenstowicz: leftmost 'strong' syllable else initial). The source's own read-speech data: 89% initial; in i/u...a/ä words initial and non-initial stress alternate, even within one speaker.
711.srule: In words of three or more syllables, additional (presumably secondary) stresses tend to fall on alternate syllables -- odd-numbered syllables when stress is initial, even-numbered when it is on the second syllable -- so that words are realised as disyllabic feet (less often a trisyllabic foot); a 'fairly persistent tendency' in read speech, attributed to sentence prosody and possibly morphological structure; primary vs secondary degrees not yet distinguished, and third-syllable stress 'not always perceivable'. Earlier descriptions noted secondary stress only in compounds.
711.quote: It has been established earlier that stress in the dialects of Moksha is mainly located on the word-initial syllable. Alternation in the position of stress has been considered to be associated with the distribution of the high and low vowels: stress is located on a non-initial syllable that contains a (or ä) if there is a high vowel (i, u) in the initial syllable. No reliable explanation of the variation has been offered, except for the assumption that the location of word stress might depend on the relative intrinsic duration of the syllable nuclei. ... Data from the dialects have shown, how…

711.exq_: There was, however, some variation in the placement of stress in such words. The same speaker could pronounce them with initial stress in one utterance and with non-initial stress in the utterance that followed. ... some authors find it possible to define stress in Moksha ... as relatively free.

712.dq: Like Khalkha, primary stress falls on the last syllable if it is the only heavy in the word, otherwise on the rightmost nonfinal heavy, otherwise on the initial syllable.

712.heavy: heavy = syllable with a long (geminate) vowel or diphthong; short-vowel syllables, open or closed, are light (e.g. [ling] in xu.daa.ling.daa coded L)
712.prule: Primary stress on the last syllable if it is the only heavy syllable in the word; otherwise on the rightmost nonfinal heavy syllable; if there are no heavy syllables, on the initial syllable.
712.srule: Secondary stress on every heavy syllable (long vowel or diphthong) that does not bear the primary stress, final heavies included (H́H̀ boosoo 'bet', L̀H́LH̀ xudaalingdaa); the initial syllable, when not primary-stressed, is also marked with secondary stress, but only tentatively ('possibly'; initial enhancement, left out of the formal analysis in section 5). Placement is by weight, not rhythmic.

morph.rootq: §2.2 (p.141): "Shinekhen Buryat has two accent systems: pitch accent and stress accent. Both systems are phonologically indistinctive, and clitics are not accentuated. a. Stress accent: The initial syllable is stressed. If VV (long vowel or diphthong) are found in other syllables, the syllable that has VV is stressed. E.g. xórgan 'lamb', teméen 'camel', gasʲóon 'bitter'. b. Pitch accent: VN of the last syllable are pitched higher." §3.5 (p.147): "An independent word (IW) has one peak of pitch accent. With a particle (P), i.e. IW=P, the pitch fall does not move, e.g. axái=mni (elder.brother=1SG.POSS). On the other hand, when IW takes a suffix (SF), i.e. IW-SF, the pitch fall moves, e.g.…
morph.elicq: No statement of how accent was determined; the only evidence given is three isolated citation forms: "E.g. xórgan 'lamb', teméen 'camel', gasʲóon 'bitter'" (§2.2, p.141). On the data in general (p.139): "The language materials of Shinekhen Buryat were collected and published by the author (Yamakoshi 2002 (text of folktales), 2003a (basic vocabulary), 2006 (text of daily conversations))."
morph.stmt: §4.1 (p.148): "Like other Mongolic languages, Shinekhen Buryat is one of the typical agglutinative languages. The word stem takes various suffixes for inflection and word formation. Shinekhen Buryat does not have any prefixes; it has only suffixes." (Introduction p.137: "Grammatical relations in this language are indicated by various bound morphemes (suffixes or enclitics)"; §3 p.144: all clitics "are phonologically defined as enclitic".)

dqtr.text: 1st. A word ending in a vowel has the stress on the penultimate syllable. ... 6th. A word derived with a suffix is, as regards stress, treated entirely as a root word; the stress is thus displaced by the suffix.

713.dq: 1e. Een op klinker eindigend woord heeft den klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep. ... 6e. Een met suffix afgeleid woord wordt, wat klemtoon betreft, geheel behandeld als een grondwoord; door het achtervoegsel wordt de klemtoon dus verplaatst.
713.dloc: §30 'Klemtoon', pp. 326-328 (rules 1e-6e on pp. 327-328); cf. §6 'ai', p. 306 (klemtoon on final diphthongs).
713.heavy: Only a final-syllable diphthong (tweeklank: ai, au, oi...) attracts the klemtoon onto its first element: 'vrij duidelijk' (fairly clearly) when the diphthong is followed by a closing consonant or hamzah, variable between speakers when the diphthong is word-final open. A plain consonant-closed final syllable does NOT attract stress (penult 'in de meeste gevallen'); a hamzah-closed final gets about equal stress with the penult, 'soms eenige neiging' to final. No long vowels are invoked (aa is two syllables separated by a light hamzah, both 'even zwaar').
713.prule: Klemtoon (a very slight pitch rise) on the penultimate syllable of vowel-final words; consonant-final words also penult in most cases though hard to hear; if the final syllable contains a diphthong the stress falls on the first part of the diphthong (clearly so when closed by C or hamzah; penult ~ diphthong variation when open); hamzah-final words penult and final about equally stressed; suffixes shift the stress to the new penult.
713.srule: Not mentioned in Dunnebier 1929, §30 'Klemtoon' pp. 326-328 (whole section read, with the diphthong cross-passages §§6-11 pp. 306-308): the grammar describes one weak, variable klemtoon per word and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress.

morph.rootq: §30 (BKI 85:327-328): '1e. Een op klinker eindigend woord heeft den klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep. ... 6e. Een met suffix afgeleid woord wordt, wat klemtoon betreft, geheel behandeld als een grondwoord; door het achtervoegsel wordt de klemtoon dus verplaatst.' [A suffixed word is treated, as to stress, entirely like a base word; the suffix therefore shifts the stress.] The rules are stated on the word (final/penultimate syllable, final diphthong, final hamzah); the only mention of morphology (rule 6e) denies root-anchoring: suffixes are inside the stress domain and move the stress; prefixes are not mentioned.
morph.elicq: §30 (BKI 85:326-327): 'Onder klemtoon moet hier niet geheel hetzelfde worden verstaan als in het Nederlandsch, daar deze hier slechts bestaat uit een zeer lichte, soms bijna niet te hooren verhooging van den toon. ... Dit is echter oorzaak, dat het maar al te vaak heel moeielijk is om uit te maken welke lettergreep wij naar ons begrip als de beklemtoonde moeten beschouwen. En deze moeielijkheid wordt verhoogd door het feit, dat men van verschillende personen dezelfde woorden anders kan hooren beklemtonen ... Wanneer we ons dan ook veroorloven hieronder toch nog eenige regelen voor het leggen van den klemtoon te geven, dan geschiedt dit onder het noodige voorbehoud' — impressionistic…
